statement: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta are lost in Parkinson's disease, most severely in the ventrolateral tier and in calbindin-poor nigrosomes; loss of the dopaminergic phenotype precedes loss of the cells.
references: [{"citation": "Fearnley JM, Lees AJ. Ageing and Parkinson's disease: substantia nigra regional selectivity. Brain 1991.", "pmid": "1933245", "doi": "10.1093/brain/114.5.2283", "finding": "Exponential loss of pigmented neurons in PD, 45% in the first decade; greatest in the lateral ventral tier (average 91%), then medial ventral (71%) and dorsal tier (56%), the reverse of the pattern in normal ageing."}, {"citation": "Damier P, Hirsch EC, Agid Y, Graybiel AM. The substantia nigra of the human brain. II. Patterns of loss of dopamine-containing neurons in Parkinson's disease. Brain 1999.", "pmid": "10430830", "doi": "10.1093/brain/122.8.1437", "finding": "Loss follows a strict order across calbindin-defined compartments, maximal (98%) in nigrosome 1 and higher in nigrosomes than in the nigral matrix; the degree of loss relates to disease duration."}, {"citation": "Kordower JH, Olanow CW, Dodiya HB, et al. Disease duration and the integrity of the nigrostriatal system in Parkinson's disease. Brain 2013.", "pmid": "23884810", "doi": "10.1093/brain/awt192", "finding": "50-90% loss of tyrosine-hydroxylase-positive nigral neurons from the earliest time points studied; dopaminergic markers in the dorsal putamen virtually gone by 4 years after diagnosis; loss of melanised neurons lags behind loss of dopaminergic markers."}]
measurement_note: Single-nucleus data are a weak instrument for counting neurons. They give each cell type's share of the nuclei captured, not cell numbers, so the share depends on how much of the nigra, white matter and neighbouring structures a dissection took: in control nigra the dopaminergic share of all nuclei ranges from 0.15% (Smajic 2022) to 35% (Volpato 2025) across datasets, and the case/control ratio from 0.14 (Kamath 2022) to 1.2 (Ma 2025). Most datasets have 5-15 donors per group. Tissue is taken at death, when the most vulnerable neurons are long gone, so cases are compared on their surviving neurons, and degenerating neuromelanin-laden neurons may not survive nuclei isolation. Sorted or enriched nuclei (Kamath 2022) cannot measure tissue composition at all. The single-cell data agree in direction (pooled across datasets, dopaminergic share of nigral neurons lower in PD), but the size of the loss is established by stereology, not by these data.

statement: Lewy pathology in sporadic PD follows a stereotyped ascending course: it begins in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and the anterior olfactory nucleus, ascends through the brainstem, then reaches the anteromedial temporal mesocortex and finally the neocortex, prefrontal and high-order association areas before primary fields.
references: [{"citation": "Braak H, Del Tredici K, Rub U, de Vos RA, Jansen Steur EN, Braak E. Staging of brain pathology related to sporadic Parkinson's disease. Neurobiol Aging 2003.", "pmid": "12498954", "doi": "10.1016/s0197-4580(02)00065-9", "finding": "Alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy neurites and Lewy bodies first appear in the dorsal motor nucleus of the glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves and the anterior olfactory nucleus; the brainstem process ascends with little variation between individuals; cortical involvement starts in the anteromedial temporal mesocortex, then high-order sensory association and prefrontal areas, then premotor and primary sensory and motor fields."}]
regions: ["vagal nucleus (DMNX)", "substantia nigra", "amygdala", "temporal cortex", "cingulate cortex", "prefrontal cortex", "motor cortex", "visual cortex"]
measurement_note: The atlas uses this sequence to label brain regions with the Braak stage at which Lewy pathology reaches them, and to group donors by Lewy stage. The single-cell data do not measure Lewy pathology itself; staging comes from each brain bank's neuropathology report, and is missing for several datasets.

statement: Alpha-synuclein is the main protein component of Lewy bodies, and mutations in its gene (SNCA) cause familial, autosomal dominant PD.
references: [{"citation": "Spillantini MG, Schmidt ML, Lee VM, Trojanowski JQ, Jakes R, Goedert M. Alpha-synuclein in Lewy bodies. Nature 1997.", "pmid": "9278044", "doi": "10.1038/42166", "finding": "Alpha-synuclein is present in Lewy bodies, the defining inclusions of PD and dementia with Lewy bodies."}, {"citation": "Polymeropoulos MH, Lavedan C, Leroy E, et al. Mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene identified in families with Parkinson's disease. Science 1997.", "pmid": "9197268", "doi": "10.1126/science.276.5321.2045", "finding": "A mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene segregates with PD in a large Italian kindred and three unrelated families of Greek origin with autosomal dominant inheritance."}]
measurement_note: Single-nucleus RNA measures SNCA transcripts, not the aggregated protein that defines Lewy pathology, so SNCA expression changes (statement CS18) need not mirror aggregation, and neurons carrying Lewy bodies cannot be identified from RNA alone.

statement: Common genetic variation contributes to PD risk: 90 independent genome-wide significant signals at 78 genomic regions explain 16-36% of heritable risk in people of European ancestry.
references: [{"citation": "Nalls MA, Blauwendraat C, Vallerga CL, et al. Identification of novel risk loci, causal insights, and heritable risk for Parkinson's disease: a meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies. Lancet Neurol 2019.", "pmid": "31701892", "doi": "10.1016/s1474-4422(19)30320-5", "finding": "37,688 cases, 18,618 UK Biobank proxy cases and 1.4 million controls of European ancestry; 90 independent risk signals across 78 regions, 38 of them new; heritable risk explained 16-36%; loci brain-enriched, with neuronal cell types implicated from single-cell data."}]
measurement_note: The atlas's genetic-enrichment tests use these summary statistics, so they inherit their European-ancestry sample. Which cell types the risk acts through is a separate question: the cross-dataset re-analysis finds enrichment in oligodendrocyte identity and in genes glia and vascular cells induce in PD rather than in dopaminergic-neuron identity (statements CS16, CS17).

statement: Striatal dopamine is lost unevenly in PD: almost completely in the putamen, most in its caudal part, while most of the caudate keeps substantial dopamine; motor signs follow mainly from the putamen loss.
references: [{"citation": "Kish SJ, Shannak K, Hornykiewicz O. Uneven pattern of dopamine loss in the striatum of patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med 1988.", "pmid": "3352672", "doi": "10.1056/nejm198804073181402", "finding": "In eight PD brains, nearly complete dopamine depletion in all putamen subdivisions (under 1% left caudally); in the caudate only the dorsal rostral part was severely depleted (4% left), the rest kept up to about 40% of control levels."}]
measurement_note: The striatum contains the axon terminals of nigral dopaminergic neurons, not their cell bodies, so striatal single-nucleus data cannot show the dopamine loss itself; they show how striatal neurons and glia respond to it.

statement: Mitochondrial complex I activity is deficient in the PD brain.
references: [{"citation": "Schapira AH, Cooper JM, Dexter D, Jenner P, Clark JB, Marsden CD. Mitochondrial complex I deficiency in Parkinson's disease. Lancet 1989.", "pmid": "2566813", "doi": "10.1016/s0140-6736(89)92366-0", "finding": "Mitochondrial complex I deficiency in Parkinson's disease (reported as a short communication)."}]
measurement_note: Complex I deficiency is a tissue-level enzyme activity. The single-cell data measure transcripts per cell type: neurons show falling oxidative phosphorylation genes (statement CS13), while in oligodendrocytes complex I biogenesis genes are slightly higher in PD (finding F-q-complex1-odc). Transcript levels and enzyme activity need not move together.

statement: HLA-DR-positive reactive microglia are abundant in the substantia nigra in PD, alongside Lewy bodies and free melanin.
references: [{"citation": "McGeer PL, Itagaki S, Boyes BE, McGeer EG. Reactive microglia are positive for HLA-DR in the substantia nigra of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease brains. Neurology 1988.", "pmid": "3399080", "doi": "10.1212/wnl.38.8.1285", "finding": "Large numbers of HLA-DR-positive reactive microglia in the substantia nigra of all 5 PD and 5 parkinsonism with dementia cases, in 6 of 9 Alzheimer's cases, and in 1 of 11 age-matched controls."}]
measurement_note: Immunostaining sees activated microglia where they are, around degenerating neurons in the nigra. Single-nucleus state scores average over all microglia of a sample and region, which can dilute focal activation; the re-analysis finds more microglia in PD (CS04) and individual activation genes up (CS05) but no increase of the published inflammatory transcriptional states (CS06). That says inflammatory programmes are not broadly raised across microglia, not that no microglia are activated.

statement: CD8-positive and CD4-positive T cells are found in the brain parenchyma in PD post-mortem tissue.
references: [{"citation": "Brochard V, Combadiere B, Prigent A, et al. Infiltration of CD4+ lymphocytes into the brain contributes to neurodegeneration in a mouse model of Parkinson disease. J Clin Invest 2009.", "pmid": "19104149", "doi": "10.1172/jci36470", "finding": "CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, but not B cells, had invaded the brain in post-mortem human PD specimens and in the MPTP mouse model; in mice, dopaminergic cell death depended on CD4+ T cells and FasL."}]
measurement_note: T cells are a tiny fraction of brain nuclei, so single-nucleus datasets capture few of them and compare their shares with little power. The re-analysis finds no consistent difference in T-cell shares (CS12), which leaves open whether small numbers of T cells infiltrate, as immunostaining shows.
